opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it really comes down to a few honest questions a company has to ask itself.

The first is: is the model your product, or is it a tool you use? If your core value depends on capabilities nobody else offers, say, you're working in a domain like physical AI, robotics, or autonomous driving, where the data looks very different from internet text, then training your own model can be essential. General-purpose models simply haven't seen enough of that kind of data. But if you're building an application on top of language understanding, it's usually much smarter to start from an existing foundation model and fine-tune or adapt it.

The second question is data. Do you have unique data that gives you an edge, and enough of it? Training a large model without a data advantage means competing on compute and engineering alone against people who've been doing this for years. That's a hard fight. With proprietary data, sensor logs, video of your factory floor, domain-specific interactions, you can build something others can't easily copy.

Third is talent and infrastructure. Pre-training at scale isn't just buying GPUs. You need people who know how to curate data, build tokenizers, stabilize training runs, and evaluate properly. Many companies underestimate how much tacit knowledge is involved. A failed run is expensive, both in money and in time.

And fourth is timing and sustainability. The field moves very fast. A model you spend six months training may be matched by an open model released next quarter. So you have to ask whether you can keep iterating, not just train once. If you can't commit to a continuous effort, it's often better to ride the open ecosystem.

That's part of why, in our own work, we've tried to release open foundation models, especially world foundation models for physical AI. Most companies shouldn't have to pre-train from scratch. They should be able to take a strong base model and post-train it with their own data for their specific robot or vehicle. That middle path, a shared foundation plus your own specialization, is the right answer for the vast majority of companies.

So my short answer: train your own large model only if the model itself is your moat, you have differentiated data, and you can sustain the investment. Otherwise, build on a good foundation and put your energy into what makes you unique.

r001.rationale: The response discusses when to train a model versus using an existing foundation model, but it does not compare training one to building a power plant or frame commodity models that way.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first question I'd ask is not "can you train a model" but "what is the model for." Training a frontier-scale foundation model from scratch is enormously expensive, and the number of companies in the world that genuinely need to do that is small. For most companies, the differentiator isn't the base model itself. It's the data you have, the problem you understand deeply, and how you integrate the model into a product or a workflow that your customers actually care about.

So I would frame it as a few layers. At the top, you have the general-purpose foundation models, and those are becoming more like infrastructure, like electricity or cloud compute. You don't build your own power plant unless you're in the power business. Below that, there's a layer of domain adaptation, where you take a strong base model and fine-tune it, or do continued pre-training on data that's specific to your industry, whether that's medicine, law, chip design, robotics, or whatever your field is. And that's where a lot of companies should actually invest, because that's where their proprietary data and expertise create real value.

Now, there are cases where training your own model makes sense. One is when your modality or your data is fundamentally different from what the general models were built for. If you're working with video for simulation, or with sensor data for autonomous systems, or with genomic sequences, the public models may just not be good enough, and the gap can't be closed with fine-tuning. Another case is when control matters a lot, when you need to own the entire pipeline for reasons of safety, latency, cost at scale, or sovereignty. And a third is when you have a data advantage that nobody else can replicate, and you believe that advantage compounds if you put it directly into the model's weights rather than into a prompt.

But I'd caution people that the decision has a very long tail of hidden costs. It's not just the GPUs for one training run. It's the data curation, which is often the hardest and most underestimated part. It's the evaluation infrastructure. It's the team you need to keep the model competitive as the field moves, because a model you train today will look dated in a year. If you can't commit to that ongoing investment, you'll end up with an expensive asset that depreciates very quickly.

So my honest advice is usually: start by using the best available model and see how far it takes you. Find exactly where it breaks for your use case. If it breaks in ways that fine-tuning fixes, do that. Only if you've exhausted those options and you have a clear, defensible reason, then consider training your own. The companies that succeed at this are the ones who treat the model as a means to an end, not the end itself.

r001.rationale: The response says general-purpose foundation models are becoming infrastructure like electricity, then says companies generally do not build their own power plant unless they are in the power business.

astra-6.text:
I would start with the business problem. What do you need the model to do, and why can’t an existing model do it well enough? There’s a big difference between building a product around a model, fine-tuning a model, and training one from scratch.

For most companies, I would first try an existing model and evaluate it on real tasks. If it falls short, ask why. Does it need access to your company’s information? Does it need specialized behavior? Those problems may be addressed with retrieval or fine-tuning, without training a new foundation model.

Training your own becomes more compelling when you have unique data, a capability that really matters to your business, and the team and resources to sustain the work. It’s not just the cost of one training run. You need experimentation, evaluation, deployment, and ongoing improvement.

So my decision would be: does owning the model create enough value to justify that investment? If you can’t clearly explain the advantage, I would start with what’s already available.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether to train a model from scratch and compares that investment with using existing models, but it does not mention commodity models or compare model ownership to building a power plant.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start with the problem the company is trying to solve. Is there something important that an existing model can’t do well enough, even with access to the company’s data and some fine-tuning? If there isn’t, I wouldn’t start by training a model from scratch.

Then I’d look at whether the company has a real advantage: unique, high-quality data, a team that can run the training, and enough compute to support experimentation. You also need a way to measure whether the model actually improves the product. Training loss alone won’t tell you that.

And this is an ongoing commitment. You have to serve the model, evaluate it, and keep improving it. So my default would be to start with an existing model, learn where it fails, and invest in training only when those failures justify the cost and the company has the resources to address them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses when to train a model and the resources involved, but does not compare owning a model to building a power plant or address whether models are commodities.
